claims.claim: We identify the problem of simultaneous catastrophic forgetting of both previously learned manipulation skills and pretrained VLM semantic knowledge during sequential VLA fine-tuning, and formalize it as a dual-forgetting challenge.

We propose Semantic-Preserving Continual VLA (SP-CVLA), a continual learning framework that leverages Fisher information over a vision-language probing dataset to identify "semantic anchor layers" in the VLM backbone and applies layer-specific regularization and learning rate schedules to protect semantic knowledge while allowing unrestricted updates to the action expert.

We introduce a lightweight, task-specific adapter insertion mechanism that enables efficient sequential skill acquisition without interference between tasks or degradation of the shared semantic representation.

We conduct comprehensive experiments on a benchmark of 10 sequentially introduced manipulation tasks in simulation (IsaacLab) and 5 real-robot tasks, evaluating forward transfer, backward transfer, VLM semantic probing accuracy throughout training, and zero-shot generalization to novel objects, demonstrating that SP-CVLA significantly outperforms existing continual learning baselines including EWC, PackNet, LoRA fine-tuning, and naive sequential fine-tuning.

post.by: UAM: A Dual-Stream Perspective on Forgetting in VLA Training
post.why: UAM identifies and formalizes the problem of VLM semantic knowledge degradation (the 'embodiment tax') during VLA fine-tuning, which is the core of the dual-forgetting challenge, though it focuses on single-task rather than sequential multi-task forgetting.

While several papers (UAM, TEMPO, Anchor-Align) address preserving VLM semantics during VLA training, none use Fisher information over a vision-language probing dataset to identify semantic anchor layers and apply layer-specific EWC-style regularization in a continual learning setting for sequential task acquisition.

While PriorVLA and other papers use adapter-like mechanisms for VLA adaptation, none introduce task-specific adapter insertion specifically designed for sequential/continual skill acquisition in VLAs to prevent inter-task interference.

No candidate paper conducts experiments on sequentially introduced manipulation tasks evaluating forward/backward transfer, semantic probing accuracy throughout training, and zero-shot generalization against continual learning baselines like EWC and PackNet.

claims.claim: We identify the problem of coupled semantic and motor knowledge forgetting in continual learning settings for Vision-Language-Action models, showing that standard continual learning methods fail to preserve underlying VLM capabilities when sequentially fine-tuning on new robot tasks.

We propose Semantic-Motor Decoupled Continual Learning (SMDCL), a method that computes separate Fisher information matrices for semantic and motor objectives, applies differentiated elastic weight consolidation penalties across VLM backbone and action expert layers based on gradient similarity analysis, and introduces a task-conditioned gating mechanism to selectively activate action expert parameters per task.

We construct a continual learning benchmark spanning five sequential manipulation tasks in RLBench simulation and two real-robot tasks, with a comprehensive evaluation protocol measuring forward transfer, backward transfer, VLM semantic retention via VQA probing at each stage, and wall-clock training efficiency.

We demonstrate that SMDCL significantly outperforms naive fine-tuning, standard EWC, PackNet, and LoRA-based continual learning baselines in preserving the semantic-motor knowledge balance across sequential task acquisition, achieving the best trade-off between learning new tasks and retaining previously acquired skills and semantic understanding.

claims.claim: We provide the first systematic analysis of how individual VLM layers contribute to semantic knowledge retention versus action-relevant adaptation during VLA fine-tuning.

We propose Gradient-Informed Selective Insulation (GISI), a principled method that leverages Fisher information scores computed on vision-language benchmarks to identify and selectively freeze semantically critical VLM layers while allowing less critical layers to adapt.
We introduce a dynamic thresholding schedule that gradually unfreezes high-Fisher layers as training stabilizes, enabling late-stage fine-tuning without catastrophic forgetting.

We conduct comprehensive experiments on LIBERO and OpenX manipulation benchmarks, demonstrating that GISI achieves superior task success rates compared to full-freeze, full-finetune, and uniform LoRA baselines while retaining significantly more vision-language understanding as measured by VQA performance.

We provide detailed ablations over Fisher threshold selection strategies, profiling of inference latency to confirm that action expert efficiency is preserved, and evaluation of out-of-distribution generalization to novel object categories to validate semantic knowledge retention.

claims.claim: We identify the problem of catastrophic forgetting in continually adapted VLA models and highlight that existing continual learning methods fail to account for the heterogeneous knowledge structure (semantic, visuomotor binding, and motor) inherent to VLA architectures.

We propose Structured Elastic Weight Consolidation for VLAs (SEWC-VLA), which computes separate Fisher information matrices for semantic, visuomotor binding, and action expert parameter groups, enabling layer-type-specific consolidation strengths that protect semantic knowledge while allowing action experts to adapt freely.

We introduce a lightweight knowledge probe mechanism that periodically monitors semantic and motor knowledge retention during training and adaptively adjusts consolidation strengths in response to detected degradation.

We construct a continual robotic manipulation benchmark spanning 10 sequential task additions across both simulated (RLBench) and real robot settings, and demonstrate that SEWC-VLA significantly outperforms existing continual learning baselines (EWC, PackNet, LoRA fine-tuning) in per-task success rate retention, semantic VQA probe accuracy preservation, and adaptation speed.

claims.claim: We introduce Domain-Adaptive Layer Insulation (DALI), a method that automatically determines per-layer insulation strength for VLA fine-tuning by computing task-specific Fisher information scores on a small held-out dataset, replacing uniform backbone protection with a domain-sensitive strategy.

We combine selective layer unfreezing with lightweight LoRA-style adapters inserted only at layers identified for adaptation, enabling task-specific feature learning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting of pretrained VLM semantic knowledge.

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across four diverse manipulation benchmarks—LIBERO, DexArt, HelloRobot, and FurnitureBench—spanning language-conditioned tabletop manipulation, dexterous hand tasks, mobile manipulation, and contact-rich assembly, demonstrating that DALI outperforms uniform insulation, full fine-tuning, and standard LoRA baselines in terms of task performance, semantic knowledge retention, sample efficiency, and cross-task generalization.

claims.claim: We identify that visual and linguistic components within VLM backbones degrade at different rates and for different reasons during VLA fine-tuning, motivating modality-specific rather than monolithic knowledge preservation.

We propose Modality-Selective Freezing (MSF), a training protocol that independently monitors and regulates knowledge drift in the visual and linguistic pathways of the VLM backbone by introducing per-modality knowledge retention scores computed via lightweight probing tasks evaluated periodically during training.

We design a dynamic adaptation mechanism that, guided by these retention scores, independently adjusts layer-wise learning rate scaling and LoRA rank allocation for visual and linguistic components, allowing the more degraded modality to recover while the stable one continues adapting.

We conduct comprehensive experiments on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures across LIBERO, RLBench, and a real-robot manipulation suite, with systematic ablations comparing uniform insulation, vision-only freezing, language-only freezing, and MSF, demonstrating that MSF particularly improves language-conditioned generalization while maintaining training efficiency.

claims.claim: We propose a dynamic, layer-wise insulation scheduling framework for VLA fine-tuning that moves beyond the binary freeze-or-update paradigm, assigning per-layer insulation coefficients that evolve over the course of training.

We introduce a principled combination of three complementary signals—gradient sensitivity analysis, semantic retention probes, and held-out manipulation performance—to inform layer-wise adaptation decisions during action expert training.

We design a lightweight meta-policy that learns to schedule each layer's adaptation strategy (frozen, LoRA-adapted, or fully fine-tuned) across training phases, jointly optimizing for semantic knowledge retention and downstream control performance.

We conduct extensive experiments on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures across LIBERO, RLBench, and real robot tasks, demonstrating that our dynamic scheduling approach achieves superior manipulation success rates and faster convergence while preserving significantly more of the pretrained VLM's semantic capabilities compared to static insulation baselines, including improved zero-shot generalization to novel objects and instructions.

We develop a novel "reasoning hotspot" supervision signal derived from attention entropy and gradient magnitude during training, providing an auxiliary learning signal that guides the model toward allocating deep recurrence where it matters most.

We provide extensive empirical evaluation comparing uniform and adaptive recurrence allocation at matched FLOP budgets across multiple reasoning benchmarks (MATH, ARC, GSM8K), demonstrating 15–25% efficiency gains at equivalent accuracy.

We present interpretability analyses of learned allocation patterns, verifying that high-depth tokens correspond to genuinely difficult reasoning steps, and ablations against simple heuristics to validate the necessity of the learned predictor.

We measure wall-clock speedups from adaptive allocation on real hardware and test the generalization of learned allocation patterns across domains, demonstrating the practical applicability of our approach.

We curate dynamic spatial annotation datasets and propose a training pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning on video-based spatial-temporal tasks (moving object distance estimation, velocity estimation, trajectory prediction) with GRPO reinforcement learning for spatial-temporal chain-of-thought reasoning.

We conduct comprehensive experiments across four diverse benchmarks—dynamic object distance estimation (nuScenes), moving object trajectory prediction (Kinetics-spatial splits), robot manipulation planning (RLBench), and causal spatial-temporal video question answering (EgoSchema)—demonstrating consistent improvements over both static spatial reasoning models and existing video understanding models.

None of the candidate papers conduct comprehensive experiments specifically measuring cross-language transfer effects in multilingual SWE-agent training or demonstrate that multilingual training improves Python-specific performance.

pre.by: MEnvAgent: Scalable Polyglot Environment Construction for Verifiable Software Engineering
pre.why: MEnvAgent introduces MEnvBench with 1,000 tasks across 10 languages including Java, TypeScript, Rust, and Go, and SWE-Sharp-Bench addresses C#; together these establish non-Python SE evaluation benchmarks, with MEnvAgent most directly covering the four claimed languages.

post.why: While SWE-Next addresses scalable environment construction and Open-SWE-Traces covers multiple languages, neither specifically extends SWE-smith's execution environment construction pipeline with language-specific Dockerized build/test toolchains for Java, TypeScript, Rust, and Go in the manner described.

No candidate paper develops language-agnostic AST-level fault injection strategies adapted per language semantics; Socratic-SWE uses trace-derived skill-guided task generation, and SWE-smith's mutations are Python-specific, while the other papers use real PRs rather than synthetic fault injection.

Open-SWE-Traces generates multilingual trajectories from real PRs across nine languages but does not introduce a unified cross-language task format for synthetic fault-injected instances nor generate ~40k synthetic non-Python task instances from AST mutations.

From SWE-ZERO to SWE-HERO shows that Python-only training transfers to non-Python tasks, and Open-SWE-Traces trains on multilingual data, but neither conducts the specific comprehensive cross-language transfer ablation study proposed (multilingual synthetic training improving Python performance and vice versa with controlled experiments), so no single paper fully establishes this claim.

Active-SWE covers eight languages and BeyondSWE covers broader tasks, but neither establishes dedicated open benchmarks and held-out evaluation sets specifically for Java, TypeScript, Rust, and Go automated software engineering in the manner proposed, with synthetic task instances from fault injection.

claims.claim: We extend the SWE-smith task generation pipeline beyond Python to support four additional programming languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, and Rust) by building language-specific containerized execution environments, adapting AST-based mutation engines for each language, and standardizing cross-language trajectory collection.

We generate a large-scale multilingual software engineering training dataset of approximately 40,000 task instances (∼10,000 per language) drawn from over 50 repositories per language, representing the first scalable, multi-language benchmark and training corpus for LM-based bug fixing.

We construct new held-out evaluation benchmarks of 100 verified instances each for JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, and Rust, sourced from popular open-source repositories, enabling rigorous assessment of LM agents beyond the Python-centric SWE-bench.

We conduct a comprehensive empirical study of cross-lingual transfer in software engineering agents by fine-tuning a 32B parameter model under Python-only, target-language-only, and combined multilingual training regimes, revealing whether multilingual training improves or degrades performance on individual languages and characterizing language-specific failure modes through stratified error analysis.

post.why: While Open-SWE-Traces and SWE-Next generate multilingual data, neither specifically extends SWE-smith's pipeline with language-specific AST-based mutation engines and containerized execution environments for these four languages.

post.by: Open-SWE-Traces: Advancing Dual-Mode Multilingual Distillation for Software Engineering Agents
post.why: Open-SWE-Traces provides 207,489 agentic trajectories spanning nine programming languages including JS, TS, Rust, Java, and Go from 20,000 real-world PRs, constituting a large-scale multilingual software engineering training corpus for LM-based bug fixing that predates and subsumes this claim.

While Active-SWE covers eight languages, none of the candidate papers describe constructing held-out verified evaluation benchmarks of ~100 instances each specifically for JS/TS, Java, Go, and Rust in the SWE-bench style for bug fixing evaluation.

No candidate paper conducts a controlled empirical study comparing Python-only, target-language-only, and combined multilingual training regimes to measure cross-lingual transfer effects and language-specific failure modes in SWE agents, though SWE-HERO notes some cross-lingual generalization anecdotally.

claims.claim: We propose a quality-aware curriculum sampling framework for software engineering training data that scores instances along three axes—difficulty estimation, diversity scoring, and learnability filtering—enabling strategic selection from large-scale instance pools like SWE-smith.
We introduce a curriculum learning schedule that orders training from medium-difficulty to hard instances with diversity-maximizing batch construction, replacing naive uniform sampling.

We demonstrate that our method matches or exceeds the full-dataset performance of SWE-agent-LM on SWE-bench Verified using under 40% of the available training instances, revealing the effective data frontier for software engineering agents.
We provide systematic ablations isolating the contribution of each scoring axis (difficulty, diversity, and learnability) to final agent performance.
We evaluate cross-repository generalization to unseen GitHub repositories, showing that diversity-aware selection improves out-of-distribution robustness.
We quantify training compute efficiency in terms of FLOPs per resolve-rate point, demonstrating significant computational savings over training on the full unfiltered dataset.

claims.claim: We propose HierarchicalThink, a three-level latent planning framework that decomposes visual plan generation into strategy, tactic, and motion abstraction levels, enabling multi-granularity reasoning for long-horizon robot manipulation.

We introduce a temporal abstraction mechanism via learned keyframe prediction that bridges high-level semantic sub-goals and low-level action execution, allowing the mid-level tactic module to generate visual plan latents at behaviorally meaningful temporal scales.

We design a hierarchical reinforcement training scheme coupled with a cross-level consistency regularizer that jointly optimizes all three planning levels, ensuring coherent information flow from task-level rewards through sub-goal achievement to motion quality signals.

We conduct comprehensive experiments on CALVIN, RLBench, and a novel 10-stage kitchen assembly benchmark, demonstrating that HierarchicalThink significantly outperforms ThinkAct, SayCan, and flat-planning VLAs in task success rate, sub-goal completion, and robustness to mid-task perturbations, with ablations validating the contribution of each hierarchical level and the consistency loss.

claims.claim: We propose a multi-signal difficulty estimation framework that automatically stratifies SWE-smith instances by complexity using proxy signals including edit distance, number of files changed, cyclomatic complexity delta, test coverage change, and reasoning chain length.
We train a lightweight difficulty predictor that scores new software engineering task instances, enabling scalable difficulty assessment without manual annotation.

We introduce a curriculum learning strategy for software engineering agent fine-tuning that progressively introduces harder instances during training, moving from simple fixes to complex multi-file refactorings.

We demonstrate that a carefully curated subset of approximately 15k instances can match or exceed the performance of training on all 50k SWE-smith instances, achieving a 3× reduction in training compute while maintaining or improving resolve rates on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite.

claims.claim: We propose HierarchicalThink, a three-level hierarchical framework that extends flat visual latent planning with explicit temporal abstraction, decomposing language-conditioned manipulation into macro-level sub-goal decomposition, meso-level visual latent planning, and micro-level skill execution.

We introduce a hierarchical reinforcement learning objective combining sparse sub-goal completion rewards, dense trajectory consistency rewards, and a novel temporal coherence loss that enforces geometric consistency among sub-goal latents in the learned latent space.

We design a meso-planner that generates per-sub-goal visual plan latents via reinforced learning, bridging high-level language-based task decomposition and low-level motor execution through structured latent representations at multiple timescales.

We design a hierarchical reinforcement learning architecture with a subgoal-conditioned options network, where a high-level policy selects among discovered subgoal latents and a low-level policy executes primitive actions conditioned on the active subgoal latent, along with a subgoal completion critic that provides intermediate dense rewards to alleviate sparse reward challenges.

We introduce a new 20-stage tabletop assembly benchmark suite for evaluating long-horizon manipulation and conduct comprehensive experiments on CALVIN, RLBench, and our new benchmark, demonstrating significant improvements over ThinkAct, GROOT, and SuSIE in task completion rate, subgoal accuracy, and adaptation efficiency under novel instruction variations.

claims.claim: We propose Hierarchical Titans (H-Titans), a novel architecture that extends the Titans framework with multiple neural memory modules operating at distinct timescales and semantic granularities (token-level, sentence-level, and section-level), enabling simultaneous tracking of fine-grained local context and coarse global document structure.

We introduce a lightweight boundary predictor that detects structural transitions (e.g., section and paragraph boundaries) to trigger updates to higher-level memory modules, allowing the architecture to respect the inherent hierarchical organization of long documents.

We design an attention-based gating mechanism that dynamically routes queries to the most relevant memory tier, combined with cross-tier attention that contextualizes lower-level memories with higher-level summaries, enabling flexible information retrieval across semantic levels.

We conduct comprehensive experiments across five evaluation settings—long-document QA (QASPER, NarrativeQA, QuALITY), multi-hop scientific reasoning (MuSiQue adapted to full-paper contexts), clinical note summarization with 50K+ token inputs, and needle-in-haystack stress tests up to 500K tokens—demonstrating consistent improvements over Titans, Mamba-2, and RAG baselines.

We provide detailed ablation studies analyzing the contribution of each memory tier, the effect of varying the number of hierarchical levels, and the impact of different boundary detection strategies, offering insights into when and why hierarchical memory organization benefits long-context reasoning.
